Yellowstone County by the numbers

What is Yellowstone County, Montana, and where is it?

Yellowstone County is the most populous county in Montana, with Billings as both its county seat and its largest city. It was created on February 26, 1883 and organized on May 1 of that year.

The county takes its name from the Yellowstone River, which roughly bisects it as it flows southwest to northeast. It covers 2,649 square miles, about 2,633 of them land, which makes it the 23rd largest Montana county by area. The 2020 census counted 164,731 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 172,692, about 15% of the state's population.

For a seller, that scale means the county is not one market. A house in a Billings neighborhood, a farm parcel near Shepherd and a lot in a small town like Broadview are taxed by the same county offices but sit in very different school and utility districts.

Which towns and communities make up Yellowstone County?

Only two incorporated cities and one town sit inside the county: Billings, Laurel and Broadview. Most of the rest is unincorporated, and several communities are census-designated places.

TypePlaces
CitiesBillings (county seat), Laurel
TownBroadview
Census-designated placesActon, Ballantine, Custer, Huntley, Lockwood, Mountain View Colony, Nibbe, Pompeys Pillar, Shepherd, Worden
Other communitiesBillings Heights, Comanche, Hesper, Homewood Park, Newton, Yegen and others
Reservation landPart of the Crow Indian Reservation

That mix matters at closing. Property inside a city carries city levies on top of county and school levies, while a home in Lockwood or Huntley is billed by the county with its own school and special districts. Rural parcels may also involve well, septic and road access questions that a city lot never raises.

How do the roads, transit and schools work in Yellowstone County?

Interstate 90 and Interstate 94 both run through the county, along with U.S. 87, U.S. 212, U.S. 310 and Montana highways 3 and 47. Billings Metropolitan Transit, Express Arrow and Jefferson Lines provide public and intercity service.

School service is split across many districts. Three unified K-12 districts exist at Custer, Huntley Project and Lockwood. Billings, Broadview, Laurel and Shepherd have their own high school districts, and the county lists more than a dozen elementary districts, including Billings, Blue Creek, Canyon Creek, Elder Grove, Elysian, Independent, Laurel, Molt, Morin, Pioneer, Shepherd and Yellowstone Academy.

Your tax bill reflects whichever districts your parcel sits in, so two houses with the same value can have different bills. When you sell, buyers often compare those bills before anything else.

Who are the major employers in Yellowstone County?

Health care is a leading employer. Billings Clinic, which the Billings Chamber of Commerce calls Montana's largest independent health care system, reports more than 4,500 employees.

The county itself is a large collector of money. Its Treasurer's property tax department says it collects about $345 million in real and personal property taxes and processes roughly 75,000 real estate bills, 5,900 mobile home bills and 1,050 personal property bills every year. That volume explains why the office publishes precise due dates and strict penalties.

We could not confirm a current official list of the county's top employers, so we are not naming others here.

Who handles property tax in Yellowstone County?

The Yellowstone County Treasurer collects property tax, and the Montana Department of Revenue sets the values. The treasurer's page says Hank Peters serves as Treasurer, Assessor and Superintendent of Schools for the county.

  • Treasurer: Room 113, 2825 3rd Ave N, Billings, MT 59101
  • Mailing address: P.O. Box 35010, Billings, MT 59107
  • Phone: 406-256-2802
  • Tax Appeal Board: 406-256-2701, P.O. Box 35001, Billings

The office also records miscellaneous revenue, issues tax deeds and tax lien assignment certificates, and handles tax protests and mobile home moving permits. You can search records on the county's tax records search or read the property tax page.

When are Yellowstone County property taxes due?

Real estate tax is due in two halves, on November 30 and May 31, by 5 PM Mountain Time. If a date falls on a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.

Tax typeFirst halfSecond half
Real estateNovember 30 (2026 only: December 3)May 31 (2027 only: June 1)
Mobile homeMay 31 (2027 only: June 1)November 30
Personal propertyJune 30None listed

Delinquent taxes carry a 2% penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1% each month. That applies to real property, personal property, mobile homes and farm and ranch property. Because the 2026 first-half date shifts to December 3, anyone closing in late November or early December should confirm which date the title company is using.

What happens to a Yellowstone County property with delinquent taxes?

The county attaches a tax lien and then allows a third party to buy an assignment of it. The treasurer's tax lien page says assignments are sold in late August, with a $50 fee for each assignment.

After that the sequence is slow and has several notice steps. Lienholders may pay later delinquent taxes on an assigned parcel only between June 1 and July 30 (June 2 to July 30 in 2027). In the final year of the redemption period, a notice that a tax deed may be issued goes out between May 1 and May 30. A tax deed carries a $25 deed fee plus recording fees of $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page.

The county says it does not give legal advice to people who buy tax liens. A seller with an assigned lien should treat it as a payoff item that the title company must clear, with the lienholder's interest and costs included.

The county's tax lien page keeps the list of certificates and the current rules, which changed after recent legislation.

How do I appeal a Yellowstone County property valuation?

You object in writing within 30 days of the date on the classification and appraisal notice. That keeps your appeal alive for both years of the two-year valuation cycle on residential and commercial property.

The county's appeals page walks through the timing under Montana Code Annotated sections 15-7-102 and 15-15-102:

  • You may submit one application for reduction per valuation cycle.
  • An objection filed after 30 days applies only to the second year, and must be in by June 1 of that year.
  • The 30 days run from the date on the notice, not the date you received it, and no extra mailing days are added.
  • Only the County Tax Appeal Board can decide whether a late appeal had good cause, such as a notice mailed to the wrong address.

After an informal Department of Revenue review, you can appeal that result to the county board, and then to the State Tax Appeal Board. Boards may consider an actual selling price, independent appraisals and other evidence of market value. Completed forms go to the Clerk and Recorder's office.

How does a sale work when property tax is still owed in Yellowstone County?

The unpaid balance is settled out of the seller's proceeds at closing. The title company asks the Treasurer for the amount owed, including any penalty and monthly interest, and pays it from the sale.

A tax lien assigned to an investor adds the lienholder's costs, so ask for a written payoff before you accept a price. Pay by the due date if you can, because the 5/6 of 1% monthly interest keeps growing.

A cash buyer can close around a tax balance, since the payoff comes out of the sale. We buy houses as-is, and we do not promise a price before we see the property.

More questions about Yellowstone County, MT Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Yellowstone County?

The Yellowstone County Treasurer collects it, and the Montana Department of Revenue sets the values. The office is at 2825 3rd Ave N, Room 113 in Billings, and the phone number is 406-256-2802.

When is real estate tax due in Yellowstone County?

Real estate tax is due November 30 and May 31 by 5 PM Mountain Time, with the next business day applying on weekends and holidays. For 2026 the first half is due December 3, and for 2027 the second half is due June 1.

What is the late penalty in Yellowstone County?

Late taxes carry a 2% penalty plus interest of 5/6 of 1% per month. That applies to real property, personal property, mobile homes and farm and ranch property.

How long do I have to appeal my valuation in Yellowstone County?

You have 30 days from the date on the appraisal notice for the appeal to cover the full two-year cycle. A later appeal applies only to the second year and must be filed by June 1.

Can I sell my Yellowstone County house if there is a tax lien?

Yes. The lien and any related costs are paid from your proceeds at closing, so you need a written payoff from the Treasurer and any lienholder before closing.

Where do I file a tax appeal in Yellowstone County?

You can file an informal review with the Department of Revenue or appeal to the County Tax Appeal Board. Mail the form to the Clerk and Recorder at P.O. Box 35001, Billings, MT 59101.

Gallatin County by the numbers

Where is Gallatin County, Montana, and what does it include?

Gallatin County is in southwest Montana, its seat is Bozeman, and it was created in 1865. It takes its name from the Gallatin River, which Meriwether Lewis named in 1805 for Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin. The Wikipedia entry gives 2,632 square miles of total area and a 2020 census population of 118,960, the second highest in the state.

The cities are Bozeman, Belgrade and Three Forks, and the towns are Manhattan and West Yellowstone. Census-designated places include Big Sky, Gallatin Gateway, Four Corners, Bridger, Logan and Springhill. The Bridger Range rises in the north and the Gallatin Range in the south. Interstate 90 crosses the county, along with U.S. Highways 20, 191 and 287.

At the south end, the West Yellowstone entrance to Yellowstone National Park accounts for about half of all park visitors, and Big Sky Resort lies partly in Gallatin and partly in Madison County. Part of the Gallatin National Forest and Yellowstone National Park fall inside the county line.

What shapes the Gallatin County economy and housing demand?

Montana State University and Bozeman Health anchor the local job base. The university's flagship campus is in Bozeman, and Bozeman Health says it is the largest private employer in Gallatin County, with a hospital campus about five miles from the university and a medical center in Big Sky.

Growth is the other big factor. The Gallatin County Triangle Community Plan notes that since 2010 the county has been one of the fastest-growing in Montana. The City of Bozeman's 2025 to 2045 forecast puts Bozeman at 87,400 residents, which it describes as nearly half the county's projected total, and a 2025 Gallatin Valley housing report credits the economy and the turnover of a young population around the university.

This shows up in property tax. The Census median owner-occupied value for the county, $604,900 as shown earlier on this page, is well above the $378,000 first-bracket line used in the 2026 rate schedule, so many primary residences here pay at more than one rate.

How are Gallatin County homes taxed for 2026?

A principal residence pays 0.76 percent of the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90 percent of the portion from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10 percent up to $1,511,999 and 1.90 percent above that. The Department of Revenue explains the tiers on its 2026 information page. A second home, short-term rental or vacant residential lot pays a flat 1.90 percent.

Working through the county median as an illustration: 0.76 percent of $378,000 is $2,872.80, and 0.90 percent of the remaining $226,900 is $2,042.10, for roughly $4,915 of taxable value. At the flat 1.90 percent rate, the same house would carry about $11,493. Local mills, which vary by city, school district and special districts, are applied to that taxable value afterward.

ItemMontana rule
Homestead eligibilityOwner lives there at least 7 months of the year
Long-term rental eligibilityRented 28 or more days for at least 7 months a year
Rate after a saleStays through the calendar year; new owner must apply by March 1
Eligible homesSingle-family, townhome, condo, manufactured home with up to 1 acre

Because resort areas such as Big Sky sit inside the county, a seller should confirm which rate class the property was in. A buyer who plans to move in will usually want the homestead rate for the next year.

When are Gallatin County property taxes due?

Montana splits the bill in two: half is payable by 5 p.m. on November 30 (or within 30 days after the notice is postmarked, if later) and half by 5 p.m. on May 31. Montana Code 15-16-102 sets the dates.

Homeowners who enroll in the alternative payment schedule for a primary residence instead make seven near-equal payments, due on the last day of each month from November 30 to May 31. Missing any scheduled payment makes the amount delinquent, with the same 2 percent penalty and monthly interest. A taxpayer may pay the current year without first paying older delinquent taxes, but money sent toward delinquency is applied to the oldest year first.

When selling, ask the title company which half has been paid, since the unpaid half and any partial-year share can affect the closing statement.

Who do you contact about Gallatin County property tax?

Payment questions go to the Gallatin County Treasurer, and valuation questions go to the Montana Department of Revenue. The treasurer's office is at 311 West Main, Room 103 in Bozeman, with phone numbers listed at 406-582-3033 and 406-582-3030. The county's tax pages point valuation questions to the Department of Revenue Bozeman Office at 406-582-3400, or dorgallatinoffice@mt.gov.

  • Treasurer: tax bills, payments, delinquent taxes, tax liens and assignments.
  • Department of Revenue Bozeman Office: appraisal, classification, corrections to property characteristics.
  • Clerk and Recorder: receives direct appeals to the county tax appeal board.

The county also advises owners to keep the Department of Revenue's mailing address current, because the notices of pending liens go to the last known address on file. You can update an address by emailing the Bozeman office.

What happens to delinquent taxes and tax liens in Gallatin County?

A payment after the due date is delinquent immediately, with a 2 percent penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1 percent per month, and a lien must be attached if real property taxes stay unpaid by the first working day in August. The county's tax lien timeline explains the sequence under Montana Code 15-17-125.

The county sends a courtesy notice after the first half becomes delinquent. After the second half is delinquent it publishes a notice in the Bozeman Daily Chronicle, and two weeks before the first working day in August it mails pending lien notices. If the tax is still unpaid on August 31, another person can take an assignment of the lien by paying all taxes, penalty, interest and costs, including a $60 fee in the timeline's 2023 example.

One detail is specific to Bozeman. The city forwards delinquent special assessments to the county for collection, so an owner can have paid county property tax and still face a lien for unpaid Bozeman special assessments.

  • August 1 (first working day): liens attach to still-delinquent properties.
  • August 15: earliest date an assignee may mail the required notice of pending assignment.
  • August 31: first day assignments can be purchased.
  • September 1: most assignments are issued.

How do you appeal a Gallatin County valuation and pay under protest?

File Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice, or take the matter straight to the county tax appeal board through the clerk and recorder in the same 30 days. The department's appeals page also describes the Montana Tax Appeal Board, whose decisions are final unless you go to district court.

To keep your right to a refund with interest, Montana law requires a written protest filed with the county treasurer and payment of the disputed tax by the due date. Taxes must be paid before they become delinquent for the protest to count. For the current cycle, supporting evidence is measured against a January 1, 2024 valuation date.

More questions about Gallatin County, MT Property Tax Guide

Who sets my Gallatin County property value?

The Montana Department of Revenue. The county treasurer bills the tax, and the department's Bozeman Office at 406-582-3400 answers value and classification questions.

What happens on August 1 if my taxes are unpaid?

The county treasurer attaches a tax lien to real property with delinquent taxes as of the first working day in August, and files it with the Clerk and Recorder. A copy goes to the owner's recorded address.

Can I owe Bozeman special assessments even if I paid county tax?

Yes. Bozeman forwards delinquent special assessments to the county, and they become part of the county's collection process, so a lien can attach for them.

How much is the 2026 rate on a Gallatin County second home?

A flat 1.90 percent of market value applies to second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots, compared with tiered rates starting at 0.76 percent for a primary residence.

Can I sell my Gallatin County house for cash with a lien on it?

Yes. The title company pays the lien, penalty and interest from the sale proceeds at closing, and a cash buyer does not need lender approval to proceed.

Cascade County by the numbers

What and where is Cascade County, Montana?

Cascade County is a north-central Montana county whose seat is Great Falls, and it takes its name from the falls on the Missouri River. According to its Wikipedia entry, it was created in 1887, covers 2,711 square miles (2,698 of them land) and had 84,414 residents in the 2020 census, the fifth-highest total among Montana counties.

Teton County lies to the northwest, Chouteau to the northeast, Judith Basin to the east, Meagher to the south and Lewis and Clark to the west. Great Falls is the only city. The towns are Belt, Cascade and Neihart, and census-designated places include Black Eagle, Centerville, Fort Shaw, Sand Coulee, Simms, Sun River, Ulm and Vaughn. Malmstrom Air Force Base is listed as its own place as well.

Public land takes in Benton Lake National Wildlife Refuge and part of the Lewis and Clark National Forest. For a seller, the spread from a city lot in Great Falls to a house in Sand Coulee or Simms is wide, and each location answers different buyer questions about wells, septic systems and winter road access.

How much does Malmstrom Air Force Base matter to the local housing picture?

Malmstrom Air Force Base is the biggest employer name in Cascade County, and the base reports about $444 million in annual economic impact for fiscal year 2025. The figure comes from the base's own commander's data card, which breaks it into $285.8 million in payroll, $45.5 million in expenditures and an estimate for jobs the base supports indirectly.

The same card lists 3,896 assigned Department of the Air Force personnel, 3,371 of them military and 525 civilian, along with 2,817 dependents. It also says 609 military dependents attend Great Falls schools, and that the base has 1,116 privatized housing units. The 341st Missile Wing operates 150 launch facilities across a missile complex of 13,800 square miles, which is why so many rural Cascade County parcels sit near government sites.

Wikipedia adds that in 2009 Benefis, Great Falls Clinic, National Electronics Warranty and Walmart were among the largest private employers. That list is old, so treat it as background. What it suggests for a house sale is simple: a good share of local demand follows base assignments and hospital employment, and sellers who are relocating on a short timeline often need a quick close.

What does the 2026 Montana tax structure mean for a Cascade County house?

For tax year 2026, a primary residence or long-term rental is taxed at 0.76 percent on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90 percent from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10 percent up to $1,511,999 and 1.90 percent above that. The Montana Department of Revenue publishes the schedule on its 2026 tax information page. Second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90 percent.

Those percentages produce a taxable value, and the county then applies the combined mills of every local district to reach a bill. As an illustration of the first step only, the Census median owner-occupied value shown earlier on this page, $243,300, falls entirely in the first bracket and yields a taxable value of about $1,849. Your actual bill depends on the mills for your city, school district and special districts.

Property type (2026)Tax rate on market value
Primary residence or long-term rental, first $378,0000.76 percent
Same, $378,001 to $756,0000.90 percent
Same, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10 percent
Second home, short-term rental, vacant residential lot1.90 percent
Long-term rental multifamily dwelling1.10 percent

The reduced rate is called the homestead rate. Eligible homes include single-family houses, townhomes, condos and manufactured homes with up to one acre of land, when the owner lives there at least seven months of the year.

Does the reduced rate transfer when a Cascade County house is sold?

No. The Department of Revenue says an approved homestead rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year even if ownership changes, but the new owner must apply to keep it in the following year. For the 2027 tax year the enrollment period closes on March 1, 2027, according to the department's homestead FAQ.

That detail matters for investors who buy a house to rent. A long-term rental can qualify when it is rented for 28 or more days for at least seven months of the year, but the owner has to apply during the window. An investor who skips the application, or rents the house on a short-term basis, faces the flat 1.90 percent rate.

  • Seller: keep your last tax bill and the homestead approval for the title company.
  • Buyer who will live in the house: enroll as the new owner before March 1.
  • Buyer who will rent long term: apply in the rental window and plan on seven months of qualifying use.

When are Cascade County property taxes due, and can they be paid in installments?

Half of the tax is due by 5 p.m. on November 30, or within 30 days after the tax notice is postmarked if that is later, and the other half is due by 5 p.m. on May 31. The rule is in Montana Code 15-16-102. If a due date lands on a holiday or Saturday, payment is timely through 5 p.m. on the next business day.

A taxpayer enrolled in the alternative payment schedule for primary residences pays one-seventh of the total on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31. The seven payments fall on November 30, December 31, January 31, February 28, March 31, April 30 and May 31. The Cascade County Treasurer's property tax page says it offers two payment plan options, including this 7-payment plan for real estate.

A late payment is delinquent and draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent a month, plus a 2 percent penalty on the delinquent amount. The law also lets you pay the current year without catching up older delinquent taxes, but any payment toward delinquency goes to the oldest year first, and paying the current year does not release the lien on an earlier year.

How do you challenge a Cascade County valuation?

Valuation disputes start with the Montana Department of Revenue, not the county treasurer. The department states that you may request an informal review on Form AB-26 within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice, or appeal directly to the county tax appeal board by filing with the county clerk and recorder within the same 30 days.

The 2025 to 2026 valuation cycle uses a January 1, 2024 valuation date. Evidence the department accepts includes your own market estimate as of that date, a purchase price within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and listings from the same window, and a builder's cost breakdown for remodels. Before filing, you can check your square footage and room counts on Property.MT.gov and call your DOR field office to talk with an appraiser.

If you disagree with the informal decision, you can appeal to the county tax appeal board, an independent board appointed by county commissioners. The Montana Tax Appeal Board is the next step, and district court follows. To protect a refund, Montana law requires a written protest filed with the county treasurer along with payment of the disputed tax by the due date. Cascade County's protest form notes it must be filed before the first Monday in June or within 30 days of a notice of classification and appraisal or of a review determination.

What if a Cascade County seller is behind on taxes or owns a mobile home?

The county treasurer collects delinquent real property taxes through a lien on the real estate, and for mobile homes the treasurer can seek a writ of execution. A county letter on the topic says mobile home owners with delinquent taxes get a chance to pay in full or set up a payment program before further steps.

For a house, the practical path is to get a payoff figure and settle it from sale proceeds. The title company will pull the tax record, and any delinquent amount, penalty and interest is deducted at closing. Selling to a buyer who purchases for cash can simplify that step because there is no loan approval waiting on the payoff.

Before you list or accept an offer, it helps to collect these items:

  • Your latest tax statement and any protest or AB-26 paperwork.
  • Proof of homestead enrollment, if you have it.
  • The Malmstrom or employer orders that set your move date, if a transfer drives the sale.

More questions about Cascade County, MT Property Tax Guide

Who handles property tax bills in Cascade County, Montana?

The Cascade County Treasurer's Office collects and bills the tax. The Montana Department of Revenue sets valuation and handles assessment appeals, so questions about the appraised value go to the department.

Can I pay Cascade County property tax in seven payments?

Yes, if you are enrolled in the alternative payment schedule for a primary residence. One-seventh is due on the last day of each month from November 30 through May 31, under Montana Code 15-16-122. The county application form must be filed to enroll.

What is the penalty for late property tax in Montana?

Delinquent tax draws interest at 5/6 of 1 percent per month and a 2 percent penalty. Taxes are delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 30 for the first half and after 5 p.m. on May 31 for the second half.

Does a buyer keep my homestead tax rate?

Not automatically. The rate stays on the property through the end of the calendar year of the sale, and the new owner must submit a homestead application to keep it for the next year.

Can I sell my Cascade County house for cash if taxes are owed?

Yes. Unpaid taxes, penalty and interest come out of the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the amount with the county treasurer.

Who to contact in Ravalli County

Ravalli County by the numbers

Where is Ravalli County, Montana, and what is in it?

Ravalli County covers the Bitterroot Valley in western Montana, bordering Missoula County to the north and Idaho to the south and west. The Montana Legislature created it in 1893 from part of Missoula County and named it for Antony Ravalli, an Italian Jesuit priest who came to the valley in 1845.

The Census Bureau puts the county at 2,400 square miles, of which 2,391 are land. U.S. Highway 93 and Montana Highway 38 are the major highways. Large parts of the county are public land, including portions of the Bitterroot and Lolo National Forests and the Lee Metcalf National Wildlife Refuge.

  • City: Hamilton.
  • Towns: Darby, Pinesdale and Stevensville.
  • Census-designated places: Charlos Heights, Conner, Corvallis, Florence, Sula and Victor.
  • Unincorporated communities: Alta, Como, Grantsdale, Medicine Hot Springs and Riverside, among others.

Stevensville's story starts with St. Mary's Mission, founded by the Catholic Church in 1841 and later renamed Fort Owen. The settlement took the name Stevensville in 1864.

How many people and homes are in Ravalli County?

The 2020 census counted 44,174 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 48,582, up about 10 percent.

MeasureFigureSource year
Population44,1742020 census
Population estimate48,5822025 estimate
Median age50.2 years2020 census
Residents 65 or older27.9%2020 census
Living in rural areas84.4%2020 census
Housing units21,062, of which 11.0% vacant2020 census
Owner-occupied share of occupied units76.5%2020 census

The county grew from 36,070 people in 2000 to 40,212 in 2010. With 84.4 percent of residents living in rural areas, many Ravalli County sellers are outside the three towns and the one city, so the county treasurer and Department of Revenue matter more than any city office.

What drives the Ravalli County economy?

Agriculture and timber built the local economy, and tourism now supplies more of it. Marcus Daly, one of Butte's copper kings, funded logging in the Bitterroot Valley because Butte's mines needed the lumber.

The valley borders the Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness, and the Lost Trail Powder Mountain ski area sits at Lost Trail Pass on the Idaho border along U.S. 93.

Five K-12 districts serve the county: Corvallis, Darby, Florence-Carlton, Hamilton and Victor. Stevensville is served by its own high school district and by the Stevensville and Lone Rock elementary districts.

Does wildfire risk affect selling a house in Ravalli County?

It can. In a May 2026 release the Bitterroot National Forest said Ravalli County currently has the highest risk to structures from wildfire of any county in Montana. The same release says more than 7,000 homes and structures are at risk in the greater Bitterroot Front project area.

The Forest Service's Bitterroot Front Project covers the front of the mountains along the main valley, from McClain Creek in the north to Trapper Creek in the south, using thinning, harvest and prescribed burning to reduce fuel. The release also notes dense pockets of trees killed by mountain pine beetle, Douglas-fir bark beetle and western spruce budworm.

For sellers near the forest edge, expect buyers to ask about wildfire risk and insurance. A cash sale as is keeps that conversation short, because the buyer takes the house in its present condition.

Who handles property tax in Ravalli County?

Two offices share the work. The Montana Department of Revenue classifies and appraises property, and the Ravalli County Treasurer bills, collects and enforces. Questions about value and class go to the Department of Revenue; questions about payments, receipts and delinquency go to the treasurer.

State law sets two equal payments. According to the Montana Legal Services Association, the first half is due by 5 p.m. on November 30 and the second by 5 p.m. on May 31 of the next year, and a taxpayer may pay the whole year in November.

ItemRuleSource
First half5 p.m., November 30Montana Legal Services Association
Second half5 p.m., May 31Montana Legal Services Association
Late charges2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per monthMCA 15-16-102
Delinquent listPublished each June, with notice of pending attachment of a tax lienMontana Legal Services Association
Redemption period3 years after the lien attachesMontana Legal Services Association

The 2026 due dates moved in some counties. Gallatin County lists a first half due December 7, 2026, and Yellowstone County lists December 3. Confirm the 2026 date with the Ravalli County Treasurer instead of relying on November 30.

How did Montana's 2026 property tax rates change for Ravalli County homeowners?

For 2026 the Department of Revenue taxes primary residences and long-term rentals on a tiered scale. Each slice of value is taxed at its own rate:

  • 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value.
  • 0.90% on the portion from $378,001 to $756,000.
  • 1.10% on the portion from $756,001 to $1,511,999.
  • 1.90% on any portion of $1,512,000 or more.

Second homes, short-term rentals such as cabins and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90%. Qualified agricultural land is taxed at 2.05%, non-qualified agricultural land at 14.35% and forest land at 0.37%, with a home and one-acre homesite on those parcels taxed at the residential rate if it is a primary residence or long-term rental. To qualify, an owner must live in the home for 7 or more months of 2026, or rent it for 28 or more days for at least 7 months.

That matters at sale. A buyer who plans to use a Ravalli County house as a cabin will face the flat rate, and a bill based on your owner-occupied class may not match what the next owner pays.

How do you appeal a Ravalli County property valuation?

Start with the Department of Revenue. File a Request for Informal Classification and Appraisal Review (Form AB-26) within 30 days of the date on your classification and appraisal notice. For the 2025 to 2026 cycle, the valuation date was January 1, 2024, and a late request filed by June 1, 2026 applied to tax year 2026 only.

You can instead appeal straight to the county tax appeal board by filing with the county clerk and recorder within 30 days of the notice date. The board is appointed by the county commissioners and is independent of the Department of Revenue. Further appeals go to the Montana Tax Appeal Board, and from there to district court.

Pay on time while you dispute. Under 15-1-402, MCA, a valid protest requires a written protest filed with the county treasurer and payment of the disputed tax by the due date. Without both, a taxpayer is not eligible for a refund if the value is lowered.

Evidence the Department accepts includes your own estimate of market value on the valuation date, a purchase price within six months of it, a fee appraisal, comparable sales and a builder's cost breakdown.

What happens to unpaid Ravalli County property tax when you sell?

The tax stays with the property. Montana Legal Services Association explains that delinquent tax becomes a tax lien, the lien attaches at the beginning of August after the unpaid year, and it cannot be released until tax, interest, penalties and costs are paid. The county may keep the lien or sell it to a third party, who receives an assignment certificate.

The owner keeps title for three years after the lien attaches and can redeem by paying the full amount. After that, the lien holder can seek a tax deed, which triggers a public auction. Bids start at the total of all amounts due plus part of the appraised value.

If you owe back tax, a sale lets the title company pay it from proceeds at closing. The deed and a Realty Transfer Certificate are filed with the county clerk and recorder at the same time. Help is available for some owners through the Property Tax Assistance Program for low-income Montanans, the Montana Disabled Veteran program and a land value assistance program for long-held family homes.

More questions about Ravalli County, MT Property Tax Guide

When are Ravalli County property taxes due?

State law sets November 30 for the first half and May 31 for the second half, each at 5 p.m. Some counties moved their 2026 first-half dates, so confirm the current date with the Ravalli County Treasurer.

Who sets the value of my Ravalli County home?

The Montana Department of Revenue classifies and appraises property. The county treasurer uses the value on your classification and appraisal notice to calculate your bill.

How long do I have to appeal my valuation?

You have 30 days from the date on your classification and appraisal notice to file Form AB-26 with the Department of Revenue, or to appeal directly to the county tax appeal board through the county clerk and recorder.

What happens if I do not pay on time?

A 2 percent penalty and interest of 5/6 of 1 percent per month are added. Unpaid tax becomes a lien, and after three years the lien can lead to a tax deed and a public auction.

Can I sell a Ravalli County house that has back taxes?

Yes. The tax lien stays with the property, so it must be paid or settled at closing. A cash buyer can purchase the house as is and pay the balance from the proceeds.

Get My Cash Offer →

Flathead County by the numbers

What is Flathead County, Montana, and how is it laid out?

Flathead County is a large northwest Montana county with Kalispell as its seat, and it reaches north to the Canadian border. The Wikipedia entry gives its total area as 5,256 square miles, of which 5,088 are land, and says it was created in 1893. The 2020 census counted 104,357 people.

The incorporated cities are Columbia Falls, Kalispell and Whitefish. Census-designated places include Bigfork, Lakeside, Somers, Martin City, Hungry Horse, West Glacier, Polebridge, Kila and Marion. The county holds much of Flathead Lake, the Flathead Valley and the Flathead River, and the western part of Glacier National Park lies inside it. Portions of the Flathead, Kootenai and Lolo National Forests are in the county as well.

It borders British Columbia to the north and shares lines with Glacier, Pondera, Teton, Lewis and Clark, Powell, Missoula, Lake, Sanders and Lincoln Counties. For a seller, that geography means very different properties under one county name: in-town Kalispell houses, lakeshore homes near Lakeside and Bigfork, and forested acreage near the park.

What drives the Flathead County economy?

Healthcare is the largest employment sector in Flathead County, and tourism is the other major driver. The Kalispell Chamber of Commerce lists Logan Health as the region's primary healthcare provider, and says the county's top industries are healthcare, manufacturing and tourism. A city economic development chapter for Kalispell also names retail trade and construction among the largest contributors.

Glacier National Park and the lake bring seasonal visitors, which in turn shapes the housing market in two ways. Some owners hold second homes or vacation rentals, and some buyers purchase specifically to use a property for stays. Montana's tax treatment of those properties, covered below, differs sharply from the treatment of a primary residence.

Logan Health describes itself as a nonprofit, 577-bed health system, so a steady pool of hospital and clinic workers also looks for homes in the valley. Sellers relocating for work often bring tight dates, and that is one reason cash sales appeal to them.

Is wildfire a concern for a Flathead County house sale?

Yes. The Wildfire Risk to Communities project says Flathead County has a very high risk of wildfire, higher than 92 percent of counties in the United States. The county also has a 2021 Community Wildfire Protection Plan, published through the Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation, which uses the term wildland urban interface for places where homes meet burnable vegetation.

For a house in the forested parts of the county, a buyer or an insurer may ask about defensible space, roofing and access for fire crews.

  • Clear dry vegetation and woodpiles from around the house before a showing.
  • Keep records of any fuels reduction work done on the lot.
  • Ask your insurer for a written statement of current coverage, because buyers will ask.

How does the 2026 Montana tax structure treat Flathead County homes?

A primary residence or long-term rental pays 0.76 percent on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90 percent on value up to $756,000, 1.10 percent up to $1,511,999 and 1.90 percent beyond, while second homes and short-term rentals pay a flat 1.90 percent. The Department of Revenue explains the structure in its 2026 property owner guide. The page lists second homes, VRBOs, Airbnbs and cabins among the flat-rate properties, and vacant residential lots too.

That gap is large in a county with lake and park properties. As an illustration of the taxable-value step only, the Census median owner-occupied value shown earlier, $467,700, would be 0.76 percent on $378,000 ($2,872.80) plus 0.90 percent on the remaining $89,700 ($807.30), for about $3,680 of taxable value. The same value taxed at the flat second-home rate would be about $8,886. The mills for your district then turn that taxable value into a bill.

Use of the property2026 rate on the portion of value
Principal residence, first $378,0000.76 percent
Principal residence, $378,001 to $756,0000.90 percent
Principal residence, $756,001 to $1,511,9991.10 percent
Second home, short-term rental, cabin1.90 percent flat
Residence on qualified agricultural land that is not a primary residence1.35 percent flat

If you are selling a house you have rented short term, tell the buyer which rate applied to you. A buyer who plans to live there can enroll in the homestead program, and the department says the new owner must submit an application by March 1 to keep the reduced rate the following year.

How does the Flathead County Treasurer collect and what is the delinquency timeline?

The Flathead County Property Tax Office, at 290 A North Main Street in Kalispell, prepares and mails the tax bills, processes payments and works with the state on valuation. Bills go to the last known address at least 30 days before the November 30 due date, and the county's online portal shows 2026 real estate bills. You can reach the office at (406) 758-5680.

The county says online payments by debit or credit card carry a 3 percent fee, while an eCheck has no fee. Its delinquency page lays out the sequence plainly.

  • November 30: first half due. December 1: first half becomes delinquent.
  • May 31: second half due. June 1: second half becomes delinquent.
  • Late June: notice of a pending tax lien is published.
  • Early August: the lien is attached to delinquent properties; the treasurer must attach it no later than the first working day in August when notice has been given.

Interest runs at 5/6 of 1 percent per month plus a one-time 2 percent penalty on the unpaid balance. The county says a tax lien does not immediately cost you the property, but it begins a legal process. Lien certificates can be assigned to a purchaser who pays the exact delinquent amount, which is one more reason to clear taxes before you sell.

What can you do if you think the valuation is wrong?

Contact the Montana Department of Revenue first, because the county page says the department determines taxable value, including appraisal, classification, reductions and exemptions. The department's number listed for Flathead County is (406) 758-5700. You then have 30 days from the date on your classification and appraisal notice to file Form AB-26 for an informal review or file directly with the county clerk and recorder for a county tax appeal board hearing.

Flathead County's protest form is meant for use only after an active appeal with the Department of Revenue. Under Montana law, you protest in writing with the county treasurer and pay the disputed tax on time, otherwise you may not qualify for a refund and interest if the value is lowered. The Montana Tax Appeal Board and then district court are the later steps. Details are on the department's appeals page.

When you present a case, the department accepts comparable sales near the January 1, 2024 valuation date, a fee appraisal and your own value estimate, among other items.

More questions about Flathead County, MT Property Tax Guide

How can I pay Flathead County property tax online?

Use the county's online tax portal. A debit or credit card adds a 3 percent fee, while an eCheck has no fee. Enter only your assessor number to search.

Is wildfire risk high in Flathead County?

Yes, according to the Wildfire Risk to Communities project, which rates Flathead County's wildfire risk higher than 92 percent of U.S. counties. Insurance and defensible space often come up in a sale.

What is the Flathead County second-half tax deadline?

May 31, with delinquency beginning June 1. Interest then runs at 5/6 of 1 percent monthly plus a 2 percent penalty.

Will a tax lien take my Flathead County house?

A lien alone does not take the property. It is the county's claim for unpaid tax, penalty and interest, and it can be assigned to a purchaser who pays the delinquent amount. Paying the balance before or at closing clears it.

Can I sell a Flathead County house as-is for cash?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house with deferred repairs or back taxes, and the title company pays the tax from your proceeds.
